title: From objects to bytes: JSON, binary formats and serializers
goal: By the end, you can explain why a program's objects must be turned into bytes before they're stored or sent, show why Java's built-in decoder can run code a stranger chose and how a filter stops it, predict when JSON changes a big number, and compare one payment's size in five formats.
opening:
Picture the owner of Fern Bakery. A customer wants a refund of 40.00. She finds the payment on her dashboard, a web page listing the day's card payments, and presses Refund. The answer comes back: no such payment.

The payment is there. The program that records payments has it, under the number 1849204436731904017. It sent that number to the dashboard, and neither program reported an error.

It's easy to think a number is a number. Inside one program, it is. But two programs never share a number. One turns it into bytes, and the other turns the bytes back into a number of its own, deciding for itself what they mean.

In Redis Cluster and production operations, the last lesson of the Caching track, we split the payment program's data over three servers, and every value crossed the network. We never asked how an object becomes bytes. In this lesson, we'll take one payment apart in memory, turn it into bytes several ways and measure each. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: The payment program sends the dashboard this text: `{"paymentId": 1849204436731904017}`. The dashboard runs in a web browser, and it reads the text with `JSON.parse`, the function JavaScript (the language of web pages) uses to read JSON. What number does the dashboard get?
options: Exactly 1849204436731904017: a number in the text is the same number on both sides
An error, because the number is too large, which the dashboard hides from the owner
1849204436731904000, a nearby number, with no error
The text "1849204436731904017", because a number that large is kept as letters
warmup.why: JavaScript stores every number as a double, a kind of number that holds every whole number up to about nine million billion exactly. Our payment number is two hundred times bigger than that. Near it, the doubles a computer can hold are 256 apart, so `JSON.parse` picks the nearest one, 1849204436731904000, and says nothing. That's why the refund found no payment. The first option is the tempting one. JSON itself sets no limit on numbers, so it feels safe, but the program that reads the text decides how to store each number, and many readers use doubles. The third section shows the cause and the fix.

sections.h: A payment in memory is a web of addresses
sections.body:
Let's start with the payment itself. The café's payment program is written in Kotlin, a language that runs on the JVM (the Java virtual machine, the program that runs Java and Kotlin code). It keeps each card payment as an object of this class:

```kotlin
data class Authorization(
    val paymentId: Long,     // 1849204436731904017, from a number generator
    val merchant: String,    // "Fern Bakery", the shop that was paid
    val amountMinor: Long,   // 4000 means 40.00 EUR, counted in cents
    val currency: String,    // "EUR"
    val tags: List<String>,  // ["card", "3ds"]
)
```

A `data class` is Kotlin's short way to write a class that holds values. This one is called `Authorization` because it records the moment the customer's bank said yes. The code calls the shop a merchant. And `3ds` notes that the bank asked the customer to confirm the payment in its app.

While the program runs, it keeps its objects in memory, the computer's fast working space, which is wiped when the program stops. Memory is one long row of bytes. A byte is eight bits (ones and zeros), so it holds a number from 0 to 255. Every byte has a number of its own, its address, the way every house on a street has one. A running program is called a process, and each process gets memory of its own that no other process can see.

Java keeps objects in a part of that memory called the heap. Our payment isn't one block there. The object holds its two `Long` numbers (Kotlin's 64-bit whole numbers) itself. But `merchant`, `currency` and `tags` hold addresses: each one says where another object sits in the heap. A field that holds an address is called a **reference**. The text "Fern Bakery" is an object of its own, which points at another object that holds its letters. The list points at an array, which points at two more strings. That's eleven small objects, tied together by addresses. The figure shows them, with each address written as @ and a number.

Those addresses mean something only inside this one process, and only for now. Java's garbage collector (GC), the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses, moves objects around while the program runs, and fixes every reference as it goes. Copy the raw memory to another machine, and `merchant` points at whatever sits at that address there. A program in Python, another language, couldn't make sense of the layout at all.

A parcel in the post has the same problem. Say a sticky note on your desk reads "passport: second drawer". The note is a reference. You can't post the note to a friend abroad, because their desk has no second drawer with your passport in it. You post the passport itself, in a box, with a list of what's inside. The box is the row of bytes, and the list is the structure that lets your friend unpack it. The picture breaks on one point, which the last section measures: on a real box the labels cost nothing, but in bytes they can be half the parcel.

So whenever data leaves a process, something must turn the web of objects into one self-contained row of bytes. Every value is written out, plus enough structure (lengths, types, perhaps names) for a reader to rebuild it without our memory. That's **encoding**, also called serialization or marshalling. Turning the bytes back into objects is decoding. This track says "encoding", because "serializable" means something else in the Transactions track.

Files on disk and messages on a network are rows of bytes too, and nothing else. Programmers say bytes on their way across a network are "on the wire". We'll write each byte as two hexadecimal digits (base 16, with the digits 0 to 9 and then a to f), from `00` to `ff`. For example, `7b` is 123, the code for the character `{`.

Encoding happens far more often than it looks. Writing a payment to a file encodes it. So does sending it to Redis, a program that keeps data in memory for other programs (the Caching track). So does sending it to Kafka, a program that keeps a log of messages for other programs to read, or to PostgreSQL, a database program. Each of them stores and sends bytes, never objects.

Keep one picture for this whole track: a boundary with bytes crossing it. On one side are a program's objects. On the other are bytes that another program will read: one in another language, on another machine, or our own program three versions from now. Every format answers four questions about those bytes:

- Can a program in another language read them?
- How many bytes do they take, and how fast are they to write and read?
- What happens when the record's shape changes? (Lesson 2 of this track.)
- Is decoding safe when the bytes come from a stranger?

Let's start with the encoder Java has had since 1997, the easiest one to use.

sections.h: Java's own encoder is one line to use, and it runs code when it reads
sections.body:
Java's built-in way to encode objects is called Java serialization. Mark the class `Serializable`, a label that says its objects may be encoded. Then hand an object to an `ObjectOutputStream`, a Java class that writes objects as bytes:

```kotlin
val out = ByteArrayOutputStream()
ObjectOutputStream(out).use { it.writeObject(auth) }   // 309 bytes for our authorization
val back = ObjectInputStream(ByteArrayInputStream(out.toByteArray())).use { it.readObject() } as Authorization
```

The second line writes the payment into a block of bytes in memory. The third reads it back with an `ObjectInputStream`, and `as Authorization` tells Kotlin what kind of object to expect. It works on the first try, which is why so much older Java code used it. Python and Ruby, two other languages, have `pickle` and `Marshal` for the same job.

Look at what it wrote, though. The bytes start with `ac ed 00 05`: a magic number (fixed bytes that say which format follows) and the format's version, 5. Then comes the class's full name, `sfz.enc.l01.demo.Authorization`, and a version number for the class, its `serialVersionUID`. Then the name and type of every field, and only then the values. That's 309 bytes. The JSON for the same payment, in the next section, takes 116.

Size is the small problem. Only Java can read this format. And when the class changes, old bytes may stop decoding: a new `serialVersionUID` fails with `InvalidClassException: local class incompatible`.

The big problem is what decoding does. `readObject()` reads a class name from the bytes and loads that class. It creates an object without running the class's constructor, the function that normally sets up and checks a new object. It fills the fields with values from the bytes. And if the class has a `readObject` method of its own, it calls it. So **the bytes choose which class gets created**, and our code says what it expected only afterwards, in the `as Authorization`. The stepper below walks through it.

Anyone who can send us bytes can make our program run the `readObject` of any serializable class it can load. The program's classpath, the list of places Java loads classes from, holds far more than our own code: all of Java's library, and every library the program uses. Some of those classes have `readObject` methods that call methods on their fields. An attacker picks the fields so that each call leads to the next, and the last one runs a command on our machine. A chain of harmless-looking classes like that is called a **gadget chain**.

This isn't a thought experiment. In 2015, security researchers showed a gadget chain through Apache Commons Collections, a popular Java library. Within months, working attacks appeared against well-known server programs (programs that answer requests from the network), such as WebLogic and Jenkins, that decoded Java objects straight from the network. A stranger could run any command on those machines, which is called remote code execution. The WebLogic hole is listed as CVE-2015-4852 (CVE is the public numbering of known security holes). In 2018 Mark Reinhold, then the chief architect of the Java platform at Oracle, the company behind Java, called serialization a "horrible mistake". He estimated that at least a third of Java's security holes had involved it.

Commons Collections then refused to decode its dangerous class, and new gadgets turned up in other libraries. The library was never the real bug. The bug is decoding a stranger's bytes into whatever class they name.

Java 9, from 2017, added a way to say no first: JEP 290 serialization filters. (A JEP is a numbered proposal for a change to Java.) The stream asks the filter about every class before it creates anything, and the filter answers ALLOWED, REJECTED or UNDECIDED. A filter can be written as a pattern:

```text
maxdepth=5;sfz.enc.l01.Authorization;java.util.ArrayList;java.lang.String;!*
```

Each exact class name allows that class, and `!*` rejects everything else. Limits such as `maxdepth` (how deeply objects may nest) and `maxbytes` reject data built to eat memory or time. You set a filter on one stream with `setObjectInputFilter`, or on the whole program with `-Djdk.serialFilter=...` when it starts.

**A list of forbidden classes always misses the next gadget. List the classes you expect, and reject the rest.** Better still, accept no Java serialization from outside the program at all. The formats in the rest of this track decode into plain values (numbers, strings, lists), never into a class the sender chose. Next, we'll try the most common one.

stepper.title: What readObject does with bytes it didn't expect
stepper.intro: Bytes arrive that name `AuditHook`, a harmless class with a `readObject` method. Our code expects an `Authorization`.

try.title: Watch readObject run code before the cast
steps: Open `SerializationDemo.kt`. `AuditHook` is a harmless class whose `readObject` prints a line. The demo encodes one, then decodes the bytes expecting an `Authorization`: first with no filter, then with a filter that lists the allowed classes.
Predict before you run it: in part 2, which line prints first, the `readObject` line or the `ClassCastException`?
Run it from the `labs` folder with the command below.

In the filter pattern, replace `sfz.enc.l01.demo.Authorization` with `sfz.enc.l01.demo.*`, which allows every class in that package (a package is a folder of related classes). Run it again. Why does `AuditHook` get through now? Put the exact name back afterwards.

code.title: SerializationDemo.kt (the decoding part)

try.expect:
```text
1. An Authorization takes 309 bytes. The first four: ac ed 00 05
   The bytes name the class: true
2. Decode them expecting an Authorization, with no filter:
  AuditHook.readObject ran, note = 'chosen by whoever wrote the bytes'
  ClassCastException, but only after readObject had run
3. The same bytes with a JEP 290 allow-list filter:
  InvalidClassException: filter status: REJECTED
   A real Authorization still passes: true
```
The `readObject` line prints before the error. The code ran while the stream was still decoding, and the type check found out afterwards. With the package pattern, part 3 prints `AuditHook.readObject ran` again, then `the filter let AuditHook through`. `AuditHook` sits in the allowed package, so the filter says yes, and its code runs. Allow exact classes, never whole packages.

refs.title: PCWorld (2015): Java applications vulnerable to a nine-month-old remote code execution exploit
InfoWorld (2018): Oracle plans to dump risky Java serialization

aside.title: If it's this dangerous, why does Java still have it?
aside.body: Java promises that old programs keep working on new versions, and a great deal of older software stores or sends objects this way. Removing serialization would break all of it overnight. So Java added the filters instead, in Java 9, and in 2018 Oracle said it wanted to replace serialization in the long run. Records, a short form of class added in Java 16, are a step in that direction. A record is decoded through its constructor, so the constructor's checks run on decoded data too.

sections.h: JSON goes everywhere, and quietly rounds big numbers
sections.body:
Text formats fix the language problem. JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) writes a record as plain text: each name in quotes, a colon before each value, commas between the fields and curly braces around the whole record. Every language can read it, a person can read it in a log, and a JSON reader builds only plain maps (names paired with values), lists, strings and numbers. Here's our payment, 116 bytes:

```json
{"paymentId":1849204436731904017,"merchant":"Fern Bakery","amountMinor":4000,"currency":"EUR","tags":["card","3ds"]}
```

Now the dashboard from the opening reads it. It's written in TypeScript, a version of JavaScript, the language web pages run. JavaScript's `JSON.parse` turns every number into a JavaScript number, which is a double. A double is a 64-bit number in IEEE 754, the standard format computers use for values like 0.1 or 3.75. Of its 64 bits, 53 hold the digits. Every whole number up to 2^53, which is 9,007,199,254,740,992, fits exactly. Above that, the doubles are 2 apart, then 4 apart, and near our payment number 256 apart. So the reader rounds to the nearest double it can hold:

```text
9007199254740993 -> as a double -> 9007199254740992
1849204436731904017 -> as a double -> 1849204436731904000
```

There's no error and no warning. The dashboard shows a payment number ending in 4000, a rounder number than anyone asked for. A refund for that number finds nothing, or someone else's payment. That's the bakery's missing payment.

You may be thinking that JSON should have said something. It can't. RFC 8259, the document that defines JSON, sets no size for numbers. (An RFC is one of the numbered documents that define how the internet works.) It does warn that only whole numbers from -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1 work in every reader. Payment numbers made by a 64-bit generator are far above that. Twitter's API, the service other programs used to read its posts, hit this with post numbers. It added a second field, `id_str`, holding the same number as a string.

**A big number in JSON is safe only as a string. Send 64-bit numbers in quotes.** Jackson, a library many Java programs use to read and write JSON, reads `"1849204436731904017"` into a `Long` without any extra setting.

Numbers are only the first gap in JSON and its two common text cousins. CSV (comma-separated values) writes a table as lines of text, one row per line, with commas between the values; it's what a spreadsheet exports. XML wraps each value in named tags, like `<amount>4000</amount>`.

- JSON tells strings from numbers, but not whole numbers from fractions: is `40.0` an exact amount, or a double? CSV and XML can't even tell a number from a string of digits without help from somewhere else.
- JSON and XML have no type for raw bytes. A signature (a block of bytes that proves who sent a message) or a PDF travels as Base64, a way to write any bytes with letters and digits, which turns every 3 bytes into 4 characters. A 3 KB signature becomes 4 KB.
- CSV has no types at all, and its rules for a comma inside a value vary. RFC 4180 describes one set, and plenty of tools ignore it.
- XML is long-winded: every value sits between an opening and a closing tag.

The biggest gap is the schema: a written description of a record's shape, saying which fields it has, what type each one is and which must be there. Nothing in a JSON document says any of that, so every program that reads it writes its own guess into its code. JSON Schema (current version 2020-12) writes the guess down, as a JSON document of its own: types, required fields, and checks such as `"minimum": 1`. One trap: a JSON Schema accepts any field it doesn't mention, unless it says `"additionalProperties": false`. So an open schema mostly lists what is forbidden, which matters as soon as you try to change one (lesson 2).

JSON keeps every field name readable. Next, we'll see what those names cost.

try.title: Round a 64-bit ID through a double
steps: Run `BigIdDemo` from the `labs` folder (command below). It reads one JSON document twice, once as a `Long`, Java's 64-bit whole number, and once as a double. Then it prints what a double does to the whole numbers around 2^53.
Predict: which of 2^53 - 1, 2^53, 2^53 + 1 and 2^53 + 2 come back changed?

If you have Node.js, a program that runs JavaScript outside a browser, check the same thing in JavaScript: `node -e 'console.log(JSON.parse("{\"id\": 1849204436731904017}").id)'`. A browser's console gives the same answer for `JSON.parse('{"id": 1849204436731904017}').id`.

code.title: BigIdDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
sent:              {"paymentId":1849204436731904017,"amountMinor":4000}
read as a Long:    1849204436731904017
read as a double:  1849204436731904000
9007199254740991 -> as a double -> 9007199254740991
9007199254740992 -> as a double -> 9007199254740992
9007199254740993 -> as a double -> 9007199254740992
9007199254740994 -> as a double -> 9007199254740994
as a string:       1849204436731904017
```
Only 2^53 + 1 changes. Above 2^53 a double can hold only even numbers, so 2^53 + 1 lands on 2^53. 2^53 itself survives, but it isn't safe, because a reader can't tell whether you sent 2^53 or 2^53 + 1. The last line reads the number from a JSON string, and it comes back whole. Node prints `1849204436731904000`.

sections.h: Binary JSON packs the values and still spells out every name
sections.body:
If JSON is too big, the next idea is the same data in binary. Numbers are stored as numbers, not as digits, raw bytes get a type of their own, and lengths take the place of quotes. Three formats do this. MessagePack and CBOR are for general use; CBOR is a standard from the IETF, the group that writes the internet's standards (RFC 8949). BSON is the format MongoDB, a database that stores JSON-like documents, keeps on disk. All three keep JSON's maps, lists, strings and numbers.

Here is the MessagePack encoding of our payment, 84 bytes, one value per line:

```text
85                               map with 5 entries
a9 70 61 79 6d 65 6e 74 49 64    string of 9 bytes: "paymentId"
cf 19 a9 b1 a3 40 7b 40 11       unsigned 64-bit integer: 1849204436731904017
a8 6d 65 72 63 68 61 6e 74       string of 8 bytes: "merchant"
ab 46 65 72 6e 20 42 ...         string of 11 bytes: "Fern Bakery"
ab 61 6d 6f 75 6e 74 4d ...      string of 11 bytes: "amountMinor"
cd 0f a0                         unsigned 16-bit integer: 4000
...                              "currency", "EUR", "tags", 92 (array of 2), "card", "3ds"
```

Every value starts with a type byte, and a small value folds its length into it. `0x85` (the `0x` means hex) is `0x80`, which means a map, plus 5, its number of entries. `0xa9` is `0xa0`, a string, plus 9, its length in bytes. The payment number takes 9 bytes in place of 19 digits. It arrives as a whole number, so no reader turns it into a double.

But look at what's left: `paymentId`, `merchant`, `amountMinor`, `currency` and `tags`, spelled out in full. MessagePack has no schema, so every record carries every field name. Here the names take 45 of the 84 bytes. In the parcel picture, every item in the box still wears its full label.

Here's the same payment in each format (the lab measures all but BSON):

| Encoding | Bytes | Field names in every record |
|---|---|---|
| JSON | 116 | yes |
| BSON | 123 | yes |
| CBOR, as Jackson writes it | 85 | yes |
| MessagePack | 84 | yes |
| Java serialization | 309 | yes, plus the class name |
| The five values as a MessagePack array | 39 | no |

BSON comes out bigger than the JSON. It's built for a database that has to jump through documents fast. Every document and string starts with a 4-byte length, and every field name ends with a zero byte. A list is stored as a map with the keys "0" and "1", and each 64-bit number takes 8 bytes. CBOR and MessagePack land one byte apart. Jackson starts each CBOR map with `bf`, which means "a map whose length isn't given", and ends it with a stop byte, `ff`. That's the extra byte.

The last row matters most. The same five values, written as a plain list in a fixed order, take 39 bytes. The names were more than half the record. But a list of five values means something only if the writer and the reader agreed beforehand what comes first, second and third, and the type of each. That agreement is a schema.

Here's where today's formats stop. Binary JSON shrinks the values and keeps the names, and none of these formats says what shape a record must have. It's a fair choice where you'd use JSON anyway and want real types and no Base64. WebAuthn, the standard behind passkeys (logging in with a fingerprint or a face, without a password), uses CBOR. For records stored by the billion, it saves too little to be worth giving up readable JSON.

Lesson 2 puts a schema under the bytes. Protobuf, a binary format Google built for its own programs, replaces each name with a small number. Avro, a binary format from the Hadoop project (tools for working through huge piles of data on many machines), drops even the number. Next, we'll see how the programs on both sides can change their records without breaking each other.

try.title: Measure one record five ways
steps: Run `SizesDemo` from the `labs` folder. It encodes the payment as JSON, CBOR, MessagePack and Java serialization, then encodes the five values alone, as a list.
Find the field names in the MessagePack hex: `70 61 79 6d 65 6e 74 49 64` is `paymentId`, one byte per letter.
Change `tags` to ten tags and run it again. Which format grows the least for each tag, and why?

code.title: SizesDemo.kt (the measuring part)
code.src:
val auth = Authorization(1849204436731904017, "Fern Bakery", 4000, "EUR", listOf("card", "3ds"))
show("JSON", json.writeValueAsBytes(auth))
show("CBOR", cbor.writeValueAsBytes(auth))
show("MessagePack", msgpack.writeValueAsBytes(auth))
show("Java serialization", ByteArrayOutputStream().also { ObjectOutputStream(it).use { o -> o.writeObject(auth) } }.toByteArray())

// the same five values with no field names, as an array
val values = listOf(auth.paymentId, auth.merchant, auth.amountMinor, auth.currency, auth.tags)
show("JSON, no names", json.writeValueAsBytes(values))
show("MessagePack, no names", msgpack.writeValueAsBytes(values))

try.expect:
```text
JSON                    116 bytes   7b 22 70 61 79 6d 65 6e 74 49 64 22 3a 31 38 34 ...
CBOR                     85 bytes   bf 69 70 61 79 6d 65 6e 74 49 64 1b 19 a9 b1 a3 ...
MessagePack              84 bytes   85 a9 70 61 79 6d 65 6e 74 49 64 cf 19 a9 b1 a3 ...
Java serialization      309 bytes   ac ed 00 05 73 72 00 1e 73 66 7a 2e 65 6e 63 2e ...

JSON, no names           61 bytes   5b 31 38 34 39 32 30 34 34 33 36 37 33 31 39 30 ...
MessagePack, no names    39 bytes   95 cf 19 a9 b1 a3 40 7b 40 11 ab 46 65 72 6e 20 ...
```
(the first line of the output, the JSON text, is trimmed). On JDK 24 or newer (Java version 24 and later), msgpack-core, the MessagePack library, also prints a `WARNING` about `sun.misc.Unsafe`, an old part of Java it uses; it's harmless. With ten tags, every format grows by about the same few bytes per tag, because a tag is a value, not a field name. A name costs once per field, not once per item in a list.

worked.title: Put a filter on an old program that must keep accepting Java objects

steps.say: An old program still sends the payment program `Authorization` objects in Java serialization, and it can't be changed yet. First find out which classes a real message holds. Install a filter that prints every class it's asked about and answers UNDECIDED, so nothing changes yet, and decode one saved message. (Strings never reach a filter, so they don't show up.)

Turn that list into a pattern. Put the limits first, name each class exactly, and end with `!*`. The `Object[]` line is the `ArrayList` checking the array it's about to create. An array is checked by the type of its items, so allow `java.lang.Object`. Size `maxdepth` and `maxbytes` from real messages, with room to spare.

Install it on the stream that reads from the network, before the first `readObject`. A filter for the whole program, set with `-Djdk.serialFilter`, would also work. But it covers every stream in the program, including streams that libraries open for their own reasons.

Prove it with a test: encode an unlisted class whose `readObject` counts its calls, decode it, and expect `InvalidClassException` with the counter still at zero. The lab's `Tripwire` test does exactly this. Then plan to replace the format. The filter limits the damage, and JSON, or a format from lesson 2, removes the cause.

lab.title: Measure one payment four ways, catch the 2^53 bug, and filter a decoder
steps: Run the tests once from the `labs` folder. All 16 fail with `NotImplementedError`, Kotlin's error for code nobody has written yet. You don't need Docker, the tool other labs use to start databases: everything runs inside the JVM.

In `Formats.kt`, write `encode`, with one branch per format. Three of them are a single `writeValueAsBytes` call, and one uses an `ObjectOutputStream`. Then write `positional`, the five values in the order the class declares them. The five `FormatsTest` tests check the exact sizes from the lesson: 116, 85, 84, about 300, and 61 and 39 without names.

In `JsonIds.kt`, write `isSafe`, `changedByDouble` and `countChanged`. Then write `toJson`, which writes `paymentId` as a string, and `fromJson`, which must read both the new string form and the old number form.

In `SafeDeserializer.kt`, write `readAuthorization` with a JEP 290 filter that lists the allowed classes. The tests send it a `Tripwire`, a class whose `readObject` counts its calls, and a set of objects nested ten levels deep.
Run the tests until all 16 pass.
hints: `ObjectOutputStream(out).use { it.writeObject(value) }`, then `out.toByteArray()`. Close the stream before you take the bytes, or the last few may still sit in its buffer, the holding area it empties when it closes.

Compare without rounding: `BigDecimal(id.toDouble()).compareTo(BigDecimal(id)) != 0`. `id.toDouble().toLong() != id` looks right, but near `Long.MAX_VALUE` the conversion back caps the value, and a changed number looks unchanged.
`Formats.json.valueToTree<ObjectNode>(a)` gives you the JSON as a tree you can change, with `put("paymentId", a.paymentId.toString())`, before you write it.
If the Jackson test fails with `REJECTED`, your filter is missing `java.lang.Object`. An `ArrayList` checks an `Object[]` before it fills itself, and arrays are checked by the type of their items.

drill.title: Write the safe decoder from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson. Write `readAuthorization(bytes: ByteArray): Authorization`, which decodes Java-serialized bytes but accepts only `Authorization`, `ArrayList`, `String` and arrays of `Object`, nested at most 5 levels deep. Then check: did you set the filter before `readObject`, and does your pattern end with `!*`?

recap: A program's objects point at each other by address, and an address means nothing outside the process that holds it. Data that is stored or sent must first be encoded into self-contained bytes.

Java serialization lets the bytes choose which class to create, and runs that class's `readObject` before your type check. Decoding a stranger's bytes this way has let attackers run commands. A JEP 290 filter that lists the allowed classes rejects the rest before they exist.
Many JSON readers, JavaScript's among them, keep numbers as doubles, so whole numbers above 2^53 change without an error. Send 64-bit numbers as strings.
JSON, XML and CSV have no type for raw bytes either (Base64 adds a third), and no written contract unless you add JSON Schema.
MessagePack and CBOR shrink the values but keep every field name: 84 and 85 bytes against 116 for JSON, while the bare values take 39. BSON is bigger than JSON.
The limit: none of these formats knows the record's shape, so the names travel in every record and nothing checks a change. A schema fixes both, and lesson 2 adds one.
closing:
We started with a bakery owner whose refund found no payment. The payment program sent the right number as JSON text, and the dashboard read it into a double, which moved it by 17 without a word. Every encoding makes choices like that, about types, names and size, whether anyone chose them or not.

Open your web browser's console (F12 in most browsers, then the Console tab) and type `JSON.parse('{"id": 1849204436731904017}').id`. Then try `9007199254740993` in place of the long number, and watch it change.

Next, we'll give the bytes a schema, and ask how a program can change the shape of its records without breaking the programs that read them.

quiz.q: A program reads requests from the network with `ObjectInputStream(socket.getInputStream()).readObject() as PaymentCommand`. A reviewer says it's safe: anything that isn't a `PaymentCommand` fails the `as` check with a `ClassCastException`. What's wrong with that argument?
options: Nothing: the check rejects every other class before it's used
The check runs after `readObject` has already created the class the bytes named and run its `readObject` code
The check is switched off when the program runs for real customers
`ClassCastException` is only thrown for classes from other packages
quiz.why: Decoding happens inside `readObject()`. It loads the class named in the bytes, creates an object and runs its `readObject` method. The `as` check looks at the result afterwards, when any gadget chain has already run. A JEP 290 filter is the check that comes first. The first option is tempting, because in ordinary code a type check does come before the object is used.

quiz.q: An old program must keep sending you Java-serialized messages for a while. Which filter should your decoder use?
options: `!org.apache.commons.collections.functors.*`, which blocks the package with the known gadget
`sfz.payments.**`, which allows your own packages and nothing else
`maxdepth=10;sfz.payments.PaymentCommand;java.util.ArrayList;java.lang.String;java.lang.Object;!*`
No filter, but update Commons Collections to a version without the gadget
quiz.why: Name exactly the classes a real message contains, limit the depth, and reject everything else with `!*`. A list of blocked classes misses the next gadget, and updating one library leaves the gadgets in all the others. Allowing whole packages with `**` lets in every serializable class inside them, which is how the lab's `Tripwire` gets through.

quiz.q: Your program sends `{"refundId": 9007199254740993}` to a web page, and the page's JavaScript sends the number back to cancel that refund. Which number does your program receive?
options: None: `JSON.parse` throws an error for numbers above 2^53
quiz.why: Above 2^53, doubles are 2 apart, so the odd number 2^53 + 1 rounds to 2^53, 9007199254740992, with no error. The page then cancels a different refund. `JSON.parse` never throws for a big number, which rules out the last option. Sending the number as a string avoids all of this.

quiz.q: MessagePack encodes the lesson's payment in 84 bytes, against 116 for JSON. Where do most of the 84 bytes go?
options: Type bytes in front of every value
Padding that lines up every number on an 8-byte boundary
A schema that MessagePack adds to each message
The field names, which travel in every record
quiz.why: MessagePack has no schema, so `paymentId`, `merchant` and the rest travel in every record: 45 of the 84 bytes. Type bytes cost one per value, and MessagePack adds no padding and no schema. The five values alone, as a list, take 39 bytes.

quiz.q: Your program checks the messages a partner company sends it against this JSON Schema: `{"type": "object", "required": ["paymentId", "amountMinor"]}`. The partner starts sending an extra field, `"riskScore": 87`. What happens?
options: The check fails, because `riskScore` isn't in the schema
The check fails only if `riskScore` is a number
The check passes, and your code must decide what to do with the extra field
The checker removes `riskScore` before your code sees it
quiz.why: A JSON Schema is open by default: fields it doesn't mention are allowed, unless it says `"additionalProperties": false`. A checker only checks; it never removes fields. Reading a schema as a list of what's allowed is the common mistake, and it makes the first option tempting.

flashcards.front: Why can't a program send its objects' memory, as it is, to another program?
flashcards.back: The references inside are addresses, which mean something only in this process, and only until the garbage collector moves the objects. Encoding writes the values themselves.

flashcards.front: What does `ObjectInputStream.readObject()` do before your type check runs?
flashcards.back: It reads a class name from the bytes, loads that class, creates an object and runs its `readObject` method. The bytes choose the class.
Ordinary serializable classes, already on the program's classpath, whose `readObject` and other methods, called one after another, end in something dangerous, such as running a command.

flashcards.front: What does the filter pattern `maxdepth=5;com.acme.Order;!*` do?
flashcards.back: It rejects objects nested more than 5 deep, allows the class `com.acme.Order`, and rejects every other class before any object is created.

flashcards.front: Which whole numbers survive every JSON reader exactly?
flashcards.back: Those from -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1. Above that, readers that use doubles round them without an error. Send bigger numbers as strings.

flashcards.front: How much bigger does Base64 make binary data?
flashcards.back: 4/3, about 33% bigger: every 3 bytes become 4 characters.

flashcards.front: Why is BSON often bigger than the same JSON?
flashcards.back: It adds a 4-byte length to every document and string, a zero byte after each name, number keys for list items and 8 bytes per 64-bit number, so a database can jump through it fast.

terms.plain: A field that holds the address of another object in memory. The address means nothing outside the process.
Turning objects in memory into a self-contained row of bytes, to store or send. Also called serialization or marshalling. Decoding is the reverse.
Classes already on a program's classpath that, called one after another while decoding, do what an attacker wants.
A check that Java's decoder asks about each class before it creates an object; it answers ALLOWED, REJECTED or UNDECIDED.
The 64-bit number type many JSON readers use. It holds 53 bits of digits, so whole numbers above 2^53 get rounded.
A written description of a record's shape: its fields, their types and which ones must be there.
A JSON document that describes valid JSON: types, required fields, value checks. Fields it doesn't mention are allowed unless it says otherwise.
Formats such as MessagePack, CBOR and BSON that store JSON's maps, lists, strings and numbers in binary. They still carry every field name.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "Our program reads Java objects from the network with ObjectInputStream, but none of our classes has a readObject method, so there's nothing to attack." Explain why that's wrong, and what you'd do.
explain_back.answer: The bytes choose the class, not our code. `readObject()` will create any serializable class on the classpath that the bytes name, and that means Java's own library and every library we ship, not only our classes. Some of those have `readObject` methods that call other methods on their fields, and an attacker chains them until one runs a command. That's a gadget chain, like the Commons Collections one behind CVE-2015-4852. Our `as` check happens only after all of that. So I'd put a JEP 290 filter on that stream that names exactly the classes a real message contains, with a depth limit and `!*` at the end. And I'd plan to replace Java serialization with JSON or a schema format, which decode into plain values and never into a class the sender picked.

deeper.body:
**Who found the gadget chains.** Chris Frohoff and Gabriel Lawrence presented the Commons Collections chain at the AppSecCali conference in 2015, with ysoserial, a tool that builds such chains. In November 2015, Stephen Breen of Foxglove Security published working attacks on WebLogic, WebSphere, JBoss, Jenkins and OpenNMS. The chain itself is short: a class from Java's library calls a method on a map while it decodes; the map is a `LazyMap`, which calls a "transformer" to make missing values; and `InvokerTransformer` calls any method by name, ending in `Runtime.exec`, which starts a program.

**More about filters.** Java 17 added filter factories (JEP 415), which pick a filter for each stream, so a library's streams and your own can get different rules. The limits `maxrefs` (how many objects in all) and `maxarray` (how big one array may be) protect against data built to use up memory, even when every class in it is allowed.

**JSON can name a class too.** Jackson has a setting that writes a class name into the JSON and creates that class when it reads (`enableDefaultTyping()`, or `@JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.CLASS)` on a field of type `Object`). That's Java serialization's bug again, and jackson-databind spent years blocking gadget classes reported against it. Use concrete types, or list the allowed subtypes with `@JsonSubTypes`.

**Zero-copy formats.** FlatBuffers and Cap'n Proto lay data out in memory exactly as it goes on the wire, with offsets in place of addresses, so a reader uses the bytes where they are, with no decoding step. Apache Arrow does the same for columns of data, which is why analytics programs can hand each other a table without copying it.

**Text between companies.** Banks and card networks keep exchanging JSON, XML (ISO 20022 payment messages are XML) and even CSV files, because getting companies to agree on anything costs more than the extra bytes do. Designing Data-Intensive Applications (2nd edition, chapter 5) makes the same point, and frames this lesson as the first half of a larger question: once data is bytes, how do the writers and readers change without breaking each other? Brian Goetz's 2019 OpenJDK note "Towards Better Serialization" sets out where Java itself wants to go.
